topic: Embryonic Development of the Nervous System

questions.question: What is the main guiding idea of nervous system development presented in the slides?
options: Development only increases the size of existing structures
Development progressively creates differences between cells and regions
Development is controlled only by genes inside each cell
Development begins only after the neural tube has closed
questions.feedback: The slides emphasize that development does more than enlarge a structure: it progressively creates differences between cells and regions.

questions.question: Why is a comparative perspective across species useful for studying nervous system development?
options: Because all species develop identical nervous systems
Because human embryology cannot describe developmental anatomy
Because it helps distinguish conserved mechanisms from species-specific features
Because animal studies eliminate the need to study humans
questions.feedback: Comparing species helps identify mechanisms that are conserved and features that are specific to particular species, including humans.

questions.question: What is a major advantage of animal models in developmental neuroscience?
options: They allow controlled manipulation of genes, tissues, and signaling pathways
They reproduce every feature of human development exactly
They remove all ethical constraints from experimentation
They are used only for anatomical description
questions.feedback: Animal models allow controlled manipulation of genes, tissues, signaling pathways, and developmental conditions, enabling causal tests.

questions.question: What is the fertilized egg called?
questions.feedback: The fertilized egg is the zygote, the single cell from which embryonic development begins.

questions.question: Stem cells differ from one another primarily in their:
questions.feedback: The slides define developmental potential as how many different cell types a stem cell can generate.

questions.question: Which stem cells can generate all tissues?
questions.feedback: Totipotent cells have the broadest developmental potential and can generate all tissues.

questions.question: Which stem cells can generate almost every cell type of the body?
questions.feedback: Pluripotent cells can generate almost every cell type of the body.

questions.question: What is differentiation?
options: The fusion of the neural folds
The process by which stem cells become specialized cell types
The division of the brain into vesicles
The movement of the neural crest away from the neural tube
questions.feedback: Differentiation is the process by which stem cells become specialized into specific cell types.

questions.question: Which three germ layers become distinct during early embryonic development?
options: Neural plate, neural groove, and neural tube
questions.feedback: The three germ layers are ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

questions.question: Neural tissue develops from a specialized region of the:
questions.feedback: The slides state that neural tissue develops from a specialized region of the ectoderm.

questions.question: What does neurulation transform?
options: A flat region of ectoderm into a tubular structure
The hindbrain into the spinal cord
The zygote directly into the brain
questions.feedback: Neurulation transforms a flat region of ectoderm into the neural tube through bending, elevation, and fusion.

questions.question: What is the neural plate?
options: A transient opening at the end of the neural tube
A thickened region of ectoderm that will form much of the central nervous system
A segment of the mature hindbrain
A layer that forms only the peripheral nervous system
questions.feedback: The neural plate is a thickened region of ectoderm that gives rise to much of the central nervous system.

questions.question: What develops from the neural tube?
questions.feedback: The neural tube is the closed structure from which the brain and spinal cord develop.

questions.question: The neural crest gives rise to much of the:
questions.feedback: The neural crest gives rise to much of the peripheral nervous system, including sensory and autonomic neurons.

questions.question: Around which time does neural-fold fusion begin in human development?
questions.feedback: The slides place the beginning of neural-fold fusion at approximately days 20-22.

questions.question: Around which day does the cranial neuropore close?
questions.feedback: The cranial neuropore closes at approximately day 25.

questions.question: Why does the location of disrupted neural tube closure matter?
options: Because the developmental outcome depends on the affected region
Because closure occurs only in the forebrain
Because all closure defects produce exactly the same condition
Because neuropores normally remain permanently open
questions.feedback: The slides emphasize that neural tube defects depend on which region of the neural tube fails to close normally.

questions.question: In the Spemann and Mangold experiment, which tissue was transplanted?
options: The dorsal lip of an amphibian gastrula
The roof plate of the spinal cord
questions.feedback: The experiment transplanted the dorsal lip from a donor amphibian gastrula into the ventral region of a host embryo.

questions.question: What was the main result of the Spemann and Mangold transplantation?
options: A secondary embryonic axis was induced
Only the donor cells formed a new embryo
questions.feedback: The transplanted dorsal lip induced formation of a secondary embryonic axis.

questions.question: Why is the transplanted dorsal lip called an organizer?
options: Because it contains a complete miniature embryo
Because it can alter nearby cell fates and coordinate tissue organization
Because it forms only the neural crest
Because it prevents all neighboring cells from differentiating
questions.feedback: The organizer can alter nearby tissue fate, induce neural structures, and contribute to organization of body axes.

questions.question: What does the chick-to-zebrafish organizer example show?
options: The secondary axis always takes the donor species' form
Only donor cells contribute to the induced tissues
Organizer signals can recruit host cells, which retain host-species characteristics
Organizer activity works only within the same species
questions.feedback: The slides use this example to show that organizer signals recruit host cells, and the induced structures have characteristics of the host species.

questions.question: What is an animal cap experiment used to test?
options: How defined signals change ectodermal fate
How adult neurons generate action potentials
How the neural tube closes mechanically in humans
How cortical areas respond to sensory stimulation
questions.feedback: Animal-cap explants provide a simple in vitro assay for testing how signaling conditions influence ectodermal fate.

questions.question: According to the slides, BMP signaling in ectoderm promotes:
questions.feedback: BMP signaling is presented as promoting non-neural, epidermal development in the ectoderm.

questions.question: Which molecules are listed as BMP antagonists released by the organizer?
questions.feedback: Noggin, Chordin, and Follistatin are listed as BMP antagonists that support neural induction.

questions.question: Along which two main axes does the neural tube acquire distinct regional identities?
questions.feedback: The slides describe regionalization along the anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes.

questions.question: What provides a major ventral signal during dorsoventral neural tube patterning?
options: The notochord and floor plate through SHH
The neural crest through retinoic acid
questions.feedback: The notochord and floor plate provide SHH, a major ventral patterning signal.

questions.question: Which signals are strongest dorsally in the developing neural tube?
questions.feedback: The roof plate and nearby ectoderm provide BMP and WNT signals that are stronger dorsally.

questions.question: Why can a morphogen gradient act as a positional map?
options: Because every cell receives exactly the same concentration
Because cells can use local signal concentration as information about their position
Because morphogens physically move cells to a fixed coordinate
Because gradients eliminate the need for gene expression
questions.feedback: Cells sense local morphogen levels, allowing the gradient to provide positional information along an axis.

questions.question: What happens when SHH binds PTCH in the pathway described in the slides?
options: GLI is removed from the cell
questions.feedback: SHH binding to PTCH relieves PTCH-mediated inhibition of SMO.

questions.question: Activation of the SHH pathway ultimately promotes:
questions.feedback: SHH signaling activates GLI-dependent gene expression, contributing to ventral progenitor and neuronal identities.

questions.question: Which intracellular pathway is associated with BMP signaling in the slides?
questions.feedback: BMP receptor activation is linked to the SMAD1/5-SMAD4 pathway, which regulates gene expression.

questions.question: What role is attributed to BMP signaling for commissural interneurons?
options: It specifies dorsal progenitors and contributes to ventral migration and axon guidance
It converts them into motor neurons
It prevents them from responding to extracellular signals
It restricts them permanently to the roof plate
questions.feedback: The slides state that BMPs from the roof plate specify dorsal progenitors that become commissural interneurons and also contribute to their ventral migration and axon guidance.

questions.question: What does cellular competence mean?
options: A cell's ability to respond to a particular signal
A cell's ability to divide indefinitely
A cell's position along the anteroposterior axis
A cell's ability to form an entire organism
questions.feedback: Competence is defined as a cell's ability to respond to a particular signal.

questions.question: Which factor can influence how a cell responds to a developmental signal?
options: Its receptors, developmental history, differentiation state, and timing
Only whether it belongs to the central nervous system
questions.feedback: The response depends on available receptors, previous history, state of differentiation, and developmental timing.

questions.question: What are the three primary brain vesicles?
questions.feedback: The primary brain vesicles are the forebrain, midbrain, and hindbrain.

questions.question: Which subdivisions arise from the forebrain?
questions.feedback: The forebrain subdivides into the telencephalon and diencephalon.

questions.question: How is anteroposterior regionalization described in the slides?
options: Broad early domains are progressively refined into more specific territories
All regions acquire their final identities simultaneously
Only the spinal cord becomes regionally organized
Regionalization ends before brain vesicles appear
questions.feedback: Anteroposterior regionalization is progressive: broad early domains are later refined into more specific territories.

questions.question: Which signals are presented as contributing to anteroposterior patterning?
questions.feedback: The slides identify WNT, FGF, and retinoic acid as contributors to anteroposterior patterning.

questions.question: Why is the simple WNT/FGF/retinoic-acid model not sufficient for the anterior nervous system?
options: Because the anterior nervous system is structurally complex and depends on multiple local organizing centers
Because morphogens are completely absent from the anterior nervous system
Because anterior neural cells do not express genes
Because only the spinal cord responds to extracellular signals
questions.feedback: The slides state that anterior patterning is more complex and cannot be described by a single anteroposterior gradient alone.

questions.question: What are rhombomeres?
options: Transient developmental segments of the hindbrain
Openings at the ends of the neural tube
Clusters of neural crest cells outside the embryo
questions.feedback: Rhombomeres are transient developmental segments of the hindbrain that are later reorganized into mature hindbrain structures.

questions.question: How do Hox genes contribute to hindbrain regionalization?
options: Different combinations of Hox genes define distinct developmental domains
Each Hox gene independently forms exactly one adult nucleus
Hox genes prevent cells from responding to morphogens
All rhombomeres express the same Hox combination
questions.feedback: The slides emphasize combinatorial Hox expression: different regional combinations help define distinct developmental domains and neuronal identities.

questions.question: What general sequence links extracellular signals to the formation of distinct brain regions?
options: Extracellular signals → intracellular pathways → changes in gene expression → developmental programs
Gene expression → fertilization → neurulation → extracellular signals
Cell death → neural crest → germ layers → morphogens
Adult activity → stem-cell potency → organizer formation
questions.feedback: Morphogens and other extracellular signals activate intracellular pathways that modify gene expression and initiate developmental programs.

questions.question: Where is the isthmic organizer located?
options: At the boundary between the developing midbrain and hindbrain
At the caudal end of the spinal cord
At the boundary between ectoderm and endoderm
questions.feedback: The isthmus is located at the developing midbrain-hindbrain boundary.

questions.question: Which signaling molecules are especially associated with the isthmic organizer in the slides?
questions.feedback: The isthmic organizer is described as releasing signaling molecules especially WNT1 and FGF8.

questions.question: What does the Wnt1 loss-of-function example at the isthmic organizer show?
options: Loss of Wnt1 expands the entire forebrain
Much of the developing mesencephalon and rostral metencephalon is lost
Wnt1 loss produces a second somatosensory cortex
Wnt1 is required only for neural crest migration
questions.feedback: The image tooltip states that Wnt1 mutant mice lose much of the developing mesencephalon and rostral metencephalon.

questions.question: Which extracellular signals are highlighted in early neocortical regionalization?
options: Anterior FGF8 and dorsocaudal WNT/BMP signals
Only retinoic acid from the spinal cord
questions.feedback: The slides describe FGF8 from the anterior region and WNT/BMP signals from dorsocaudal regions as sources of positional information for the developing neocortex.

questions.question: What happens when anterior FGF8 signaling is increased experimentally in the developing neocortex?
options: Cortical area boundaries shift only dorsally
questions.feedback: Increasing anterior FGF8 shifts cortical area boundaries posteriorly.

questions.question: What can an ectopic posterior source of FGF8 produce?
options: A second, partially duplicated cortical map
Transformation of cortex into spinal cord
questions.feedback: The slides describe an ectopic posterior FGF8 source as capable of generating a second, partially duplicated cortical map, including another somatosensory area.

questions.question: How are Emx2 and Pax6 expressed across the developing neocortex?
options: At identical levels in every cortical progenitor
Only after cortical areas are fully mature
questions.feedback: Emx2 and Pax6 are presented as transcription factors expressed in approximately opposing gradients across the developing neocortex.

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes the integrated view of protomap and protocortex hypotheses?
options: Cortical areas are determined entirely by thalamic inputs
Cortical areas are fully fixed before any sensory input arrives
Intrinsic patterning establishes early regional biases, while thalamic inputs and activity refine the cortical map
Neither intrinsic patterning nor thalamic input contributes to cortical regionalization
questions.feedback: The slides integrate the two classical hypotheses: intrinsic patterning establishes early biases, and thalamic inputs and activity refine the developing cortical map.
